analysis.one_liner: Requires social media platforms to verify users' ages, get parental consent for minors, and restrict algorithmic feeds for teens.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 10 cosponsors split evenly between the parties, but it never got a hearing, markup, or vote in the Senate Commerce Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require social media platforms to verify the age of every account holder, block children under 13 from using accounts, and require a parent or guardian's consent before creating an account for a 13-to-17-year-old, which the parent could later revoke. It would also bar platforms from using a person's data in their recommendation algorithms — the systems that decide what shows up in your feed — unless the person is verified as 18 or older. To make verification easier, the Commerce Department would run a voluntary, free pilot program for a secure digital ID, and the FTC and state attorneys general would enforce the rules. The bill died in committee without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents of teens and children, and minors themselves. Parents would gain the power to approve or revoke their child's social media account, and teens under 18 would stop being fed content chosen by algorithms trained on their personal data. Platforms could not reuse or retain the information collected to verify ages, and users could use a free, voluntary government-issued digital ID rather than handing documents to each platform.

how_it_helps.text: Platforms must verify the age of account holders using steps beyond simply trusting a user's self-reported birthday, and children under 13 may not hold accounts at all.
A parent or guardian must affirmatively consent to an account for any 13-to-17-year-old, can revoke that consent, and the platform must then disable the child's account.
Platforms may not use a user's personal data in an algorithmic recommendation system unless the user is verified as 18 or older, cutting teens off from feeds engineered around their data.

Information collected for age verification and parental consent cannot be used for any other purpose, and a voluntary, no-cost federal digital ID pilot would let people verify age or parent-child relationships without sharing underlying documents with platforms.
The FTC and state attorneys general can enforce the rules, with civil penalties for platforms that knowingly or repeatedly violate them.

analysis.who_pays: Social media platforms, which would bear the cost and engineering burden of age verification for all users, lose the engagement and ad-targeting they get from minors, and face FTC and state-level lawsuits with per-day and per-user penalties. Users in general would face an added step of verifying their age to keep using their accounts, though the bill prohibits requiring government-issued ID specifically.
analysis.who_pays_short: Social media platforms and all users' convenience

drawbacks.text: Age verification for every account holder means hundreds of millions of users would have to prove their age online, a burden that raises privacy and security risks even though the bill bars platforms from using or keeping verification data for other purposes.

The bill creates a new federal digital identification credential through the Commerce Department; even with its limits on retention, disclosure, and use (it could not be used for benefits eligibility or legal status), it expands the government's role in online identity, which privacy advocates worry could normalize digital ID requirements beyond social media.

A good-faith objection supporters must weigh: sweeping restrictions on minors' accounts and algorithmic feeds could push determined kids onto platforms with no rules at all, and could cut off some 13-to-17-year-olds from communities and resources they rely on, especially where a parent will not consent. The bill itself contains no carve-out for those cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside for families is real and targeted: parental control over teen accounts and an end to algorithmic feeds built on minors' personal data, with strict limits on what platforms can do with verification data. The costs are also real — universal age verification is a heavy lift, the effectiveness of parental consent depends on households where consent is not forthcoming, and the federal digital ID pilot, though heavily privacy-protected on paper, creates new infrastructure whose security would only be as good as its execution. This is a serious bill with genuine design tradeoffs, not a giveaway, and it died without those tradeoffs ever being debated on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which took no further action on it, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on April 26, 2023 by Senator Schatz together with Senators Cotton, Murphy, and Britt, pairing two Democrats and two Republicans as original sponsors.
It attracted 10 cosponsors — 5 of 49 Senate Republicans and 5 of 48 Senate Democrats.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the day it was introduced.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Social media platforms came out ahead: they kept the status quo, including teen engagement and data-driven algorithmic feeds, with no new verification, consent, or enforcement obligations. Families gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Social media platforms, which kept the status quo

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan group of original cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. Tom Cotton, Sen. Chris Murphy, and Sen. Katie Britt
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced, two Republicans and two Democrats in total.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Major social media platforms and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Publicly fought age-verification and minors' account restrictions in state legislatures and in Congress, arguing they burden all users and can be evaded.

sides.party_line_note: Support was evenly split by party at introduction — the bill was carried by two Democrats and two Republicans and drew 5 cosponsors from each party — so its death in committee was not a partisan vote; it never came to one.

industries.note: Platforms would have to verify ages for every account, obtain and honor parental consent for teen accounts, stop using personal data in recommendation algorithms for anyone under 18, and face FTC and state attorney general enforcement with civil penalties. Their core business — maximizing engagement and targeted advertising — depends on exactly the teen data flows and algorithmic feeds this bill restricts.

industries.industry: Identity verification and digital ID providers
industries.note: The bill authorizes the Commerce Secretary to contract with private identity verification technology providers and gives platforms a legal safe harbor if they verify users through the new federal pilot program. That would route age and identity checks for a nationwide user base through this verification channel, creating a steady business opportunity — though the pilot's privacy limits and voluntary design also constrain how it can be used.
